title: A Wise Man Once Said Nothing
author: Managing the Future
summary: Empty praise from a CEO is not merely useless — it is actively harmful, because it recalibrates the organization's standards in the wrong direction. When a CEO praises mediocre work, the employee takes it as a signal to repeat that behavior and may use the CEO's implicit approval to judge the work of others. The social contract rewards agreeableness, and CEOs who are naturally high in positive social styles may believe they are building culture, but they are distorting the signal their organization depends on. The alternative to empty praise is not to become a heat-seeking missile for failures but to practice strategic silence: reserving spoken feedback for situations where it is actually required. The CEO owes the organization a reliable signal — when something is called good, it should be good; when nothing is said, it means nothing beyond the absence of comment; when something needs work, it needs work.
points: Empty praise from a CEO is not merely useless — it is actively harmful, because it recalibrates the entire team's performance bar in the wrong direction and signals implicit approval of mediocre work.
When a CEO praises phoned-in work, the employee takes it as permission to repeat the behavior and may use the implicit endorsement as a proxy for evaluating the work of colleagues.

CEOs who are naturally high in positive social styles may believe they are building culture through encouragement, but they are distorting the signal their organization depends on to maintain standards.

Strategic silence is the valuable middle path: a CEO does not have to evaluate every performance observed or fill every social moment with a judgment — unless the person reports to them or is causing significant problems.

The CEO owes the organization a reliable signal: when something is called good it should be good; when nothing is said it means nothing beyond the absence of comment; when work needs improvement, the feedback must come.
quotes: Is there a deeper harm in the small compliments you don’t really mean? That is ultimately a question for the ethicist or philosopher. But I can tell you what these false compliments do from a leadership perspective.
When Tim's CEO says "Great work!" after the same phoned-in presentation, Tim's whole perspective gets skewed. Tim takes it as a signal that he should repeat this behavior.
With a simple, tossed off compliment, the CEO has recalibrated a whole team’s bar, and not in the right direction.
Empty praise from a CEO is not merely useless; it is actively harmful.

When you are CEO, your spoken words carry great weight with the team. Your written words might as well be in red lettering. You still feel like the same person you were before you were CEO, but your employees see you differently now.

Other than these situations, saying nothing is always an option, and often the best one. You do not have to evaluate every performance you observe, like Commodus giving the thumbs up or down in Gladiator.

As CEO, you owe your organization a reliable signal. When you say something is good, it should be good. When you say nothing, it should mean nothing beyond the absence of comment. When you say something needs work, it needs work.
